summaries.summary: Text-based games popularized by Zork use plain text descriptions and natural-language commands, challenging agents in language understanding, common sense, and linguistic interaction.
Natural-language commands create an extremely large action space, O(N^m), motivating constrained vocabularies, verb-object pairs, predetermined admissible actions, or unconstrained generalization.
The authors propose Go-Explore trajectories with Seq2Seq imitation learning, evaluated on CoinCollector and 4,440 “First TextWorld Problems” games.
Prominent reinforcement learning approaches use word-position Q-functions or one Q-function over actions, with limitations involving fixed words, language modelling, and admissible actions.
Sparse rewards in text-based games challenge reinforcement learning, motivating exploration methods including novelty search, intrinsic motivation, curiosity rewards, and episodic discovery bonus.
Go-Explore tracks under-explored states, uses simulator determinism, and has exploration and generalization phases for training policies from high-performing trajectories.
Text-based games are framed as a POMDP (S, T, A, Ω, O, R), with A containing all possible token sequences.
Observations and actions are token sequences, while admissible actions 𝒜_t are grammatically correct, admissible token sequences for observation o_t.
Phase 1 builds an archive of cells with trajectories, lengths, and cumulative rewards, updating cells for higher-scoring or shorter trajectories.
Phase 1 selects archive cells, explores randomly, embeds observations with cumulative reward into discretized cells, restricts actions to 𝒜_t, and denotes trajectories 𝒯_g.
Phase 2 trains a Seq2Seq imitation-learning policy on phase 1 trajectories, minimizing negative log-likelihood of action a_t given observation o_t.
The encoder’s last hidden state initializes the decoder, which generates action a_t token by token from encoder hidden states H.
W ∈ ℝ^{2d × |V|} maps the decoder hidden state concatenated with the context vector into a vocabulary-size vector.
Training minimizes the sum of negative log likelihood of each token in a_t using teacher forcing, while testing uses auto-regressive greedy search.
Standard benchmarks use no more than two words and limited admissible actions, while this paper selects environments requiring multiple words and sparse rewards.
The paragraph contains only the formatting marker [leftmargin=*].
CoinCollector requires finding and collecting a coin, gives +1 reward, and parses five admissible commands made by two worlds.
CookingWorld has 4,440 games, 222 difficulty levels, 20 games per level, 18 verbs, 51 entities, and observation vocabulary 20,000.
Experiments benchmark Go-Explore on 10 hard-level 30 CoinCollector games and evaluate CookingWorld generalization using Single, Joint, and Zero-Shot settings.
Observations in CoinCollector and CookingWorld contain D, I, Q, P, and F, while phase 1 of Go-Explore uses only D.
CoinCollector compares Go-Explore with episodic discovery bonus improving DQN++ and DRQN++, using authors’ code and same hyper-parameters.
For CookingWorld games, the authors implemented three different treatments based on two existing methods.
LSTM-DQN uses an LSTM state encoder and separate Q-functions for Verb, Adjective1, Noun1, Adjective2, and Noun2 components.
All Q-functions are jointly trained with DQN and ε-greedy exploration, with argmax outputs concatenated and <s> denoting absent words.
LSTM-DQN+ADM matches LSTM-DQN but samples ε-greedy random actions from admissible actions instead of sampling each word separately.
DRRN scores admissible actions using LSTM-encoded observations, summed action-token embeddings, and a Q value defined by their dot product.
At testing time, DRRN chooses the action with the highest Q value.
All games use 50 maximum steps, Go-Explore cells use 50 dimensional pre-trained GloVe BIBREF36 vectors plus cumulative reward, and LSTM hidden state is 300.
CoinCollector compares frames and score, with Go-Explore counting restoration actions; phase 1 uses approximately half the interactions and finds optimal 30 steps.
CookingWorld evaluates single, joint, and zero-shot settings by final score sums and trajectory length; phase 1 achieves 19,530 with 47,562 steps.
In single CookingWorld, Seq2Seq trained on phase 1 Go-Explore trajectories achieves the highest score but is 9.4% lower than phase 1.
In joint CookingWorld, one model trains on all games, all models perform lower, shuffled curriculum works better, and baselines quickly fail.
In zero-shot CookingWorld, 4,440 games are stratified by difficulty, RL baselines perform poorly, and Go-Explore Seq2Seq solves almost half of unseen games.
Results show Go-Explore extracts high-performing trajectories enabling supervised models to outperform existing models, while challenges and limitations remain.
State representation is the main imitation learning limitation because overlapping descriptions require different actions, especially in joint CookingWorld with 222 games repeated 20 times.
Go-Explore uses admissible actions during random exploration, but Zork I and Z-Machine games lack them, so language models or learned policies could help.
A hand-tailored “First TextWorld Problems” solution obtained up to 91.9% of the maximum possible score across 514 test games on an unpublished dataset.
The paper presents Go-Explore phase 1 trajectory extraction plus a simple Seq2Seq model, showing promising results with improved generalization and sample efficiency.
In CoinCollector hard setting mode 2, each path room has two distractor rooms, and level 30 indicates the shortest path to the coin room.
CookingWorld complexity is determined by the number of skills and the types of skills that an agent needs to master.
recipe {1,2,3} is the number of ingredients in the recipe.
take {1,2,3} is the number of ingredients to find not already in the inventory.
open is whether containers/doors need to be opened.
cook is whether ingredients need to be cooked.
cut is whether ingredients need to be cut.
drop is whether the inventory has limited capacity.
go {1,6,9,12} is the number of locations.
The hardest game has a recipe with 3 ingredients across 12 locations, requiring cutting, cooking, opening, and limited inventory capacity.
The grammar includes go, look, examine, inventory, eat, open/close, take/drop, and put/insert.
cook X with Y produces grilled X when Y is the BBQ.
cook X with Y produces roasted X when Y is the oven.
cook X with Y produces fried X when Y is the stove.
slice X with Y produces sliced X.
chop X with Y produces chopped X.
dice X with Y produces diced X.
prepare meal is included in the grammar.
Y is something sharp, e.g. knife.
